beats.narration: By the dying hearth sprawls ნაცარქექია, the ash-raker, the laziest man in the village, who would rather poke the cold ashes than do an honest day's work. Witness, for once, a memory kept for pure delight — not every thread in the Chronicle is grief; some are the laughter a people keeps to stay sane.

A great stupid დევი comes down to the village by night, meaning to make a meal of someone — and blunders to the ash-raker's door. Where a hero would draw a sword, Natsarkekia has only his wits, which, it turns out, are weapon enough. Witness brute terror meet lazy cunning.

The devi challenges him to feats of strength, so Natsarkekia cheats gloriously: he squeezes 'water from a stone' (a hidden lump of cheese), hurls a 'stone' so far it never lands (a bird let loose), and bluffs the giant breathless. Aid the trickery — pass him the cheese, hide the bird, keep a straight face. Cleverness is doing the work that muscle cannot.

Convinced this scrawny man must be a monster of impossible strength, the devi panics. Ward the village — not with a blade but with one last enormous bluff that sends the giant fleeing over the hills, never to trouble the valley again. The lightest Ward in the Chronicle, won with a wink.

Natsarkekia goes back to his ashes a hero, and the children laugh at the tale for a thousand years. You have kept a memory of the kind every people needs as much as its martyrs: the joy of the small and clever besting the big and cruel. The night is warm with laughter; the thread holds.
